title: Ethics, Bias, and Human Oversight
audience: Clinical researchers and clinician-scientists new to AI
objectives: Apply the four bioethical principles to a concrete clinical AI case.
Name which principles are in tension and what one costs the other.
Defend a view about which principle should take precedence.
Trace how a training-population mismatch becomes deployed harm.
Decide what to do about a flawed AI tool that is already in use.

sections.name: 1. The Four Principles of Bioethics
sections.purpose: Reason about a re-identification risk in a de-identified EHR dataset.
sections.how_to_use: Read the case, then use the principles multiselect and the conflict and precedence text areas. Each has a 'Show example' button; encourage the learner to answer before revealing.

sections.name: 2. How a Population Mismatch Becomes Deployed Harm
sections.purpose: Identify bias vectors in an ER acuity-ranking algorithm.
sections.how_to_use: Read the level-one trauma centre case and answer in the text area, addressing the data, the bias vectors, and the practical consequences. Then reveal the example.

sections.name: 3. When a Human Must Stay in the Loop
sections.purpose: Decide what to do about an AI transcription tool already in clinical use.
sections.how_to_use: The tool fabricated conversation, mischaracterised patients as aggressive, and degraded on accents. Notes are already in charts, so every option costs something. There is no reveal here on purpose.

sections.name: Consider this:
sections.how_to_use: Ask which of the three cases a metric could have caught and which needed a person to notice. Subsection 2.2 makes these measurable.

chatbot_guidance: Do not resolve the cases for the learner. The point is defending a position, not reaching a preset answer.
The third case has no worked example deliberately -- it is the hardest one because the tool is already deployed.
If asked what comes next: 2.2 turns each of these concerns into a metric and a model card.
